content.p: Bevan Spencer von Einem was an Adelaide accountant who spent the rest of his life in prison, from his arrest in 1983 for one crime: the abduction and murder of 15-year-old Richard Kelvin in 1983. A jury found him guilty in 1984, after he pleaded not guilty. He was never convicted of anything else involving a death. Yet his name became attached to a much larger story, the unsolved killings of four other young men and boys that South Australians know as the "Family murders". Police believed he was linked to that group. Nine News described him as someone who had long denied involvement in multiple crimes, and the Premier said he refused to co-operate with police.
He died in Yatala Labour Prison in December 2025, aged 79, and the Premier of South Australia said he had taken what he knew with him.
content.h2: The boy who did not come home
content.p: On the evening of Sunday 5 June 1983, Richard Kelvin accompanied a friend to a nearby bus stop, minutes from his family home in North Adelaide. Dinner was expected at home, the ABC wrote; instead the boy was glimpsed running down a nearby side street, and then he was gone. His father, Rob Kelvin, was a familiar face as a Nine News presenter. Pedestrian.tv described the disappearance as happening roughly 400 metres from the family home.

His body was found on 24 July 1983 in bushland next to an airstrip at Mount Crawford, in the hills roughly 50 kilometres from the city. According to court documents cited by the ABC, he had been held captive for five weeks, and there were signs he had been washed and re-dressed after death. A post-mortem found "quite serious violence", with injuries to his head and anus, and toxicology showed alcohol and sedatives in his body.

Court documents show that police told the media at the time that the five crimes were linked, sexually motivated killings, the ABC reported. One detective said: "We have looked at the pattern in these murders very seriously."
Von Einem was first interviewed by police on 28 July 1983, four days after the body was found. He was then 38. He was arrested in November that year.

His account changed. He first denied knowing Kelvin. After scientific evidence connected the teenager to him, he said the boy had been "willingly" in his company that night and that he had dropped him in the city, the ABC reported.
After deliberating for more than seven hours, the jury found von Einem guilty in October 1984, the ABC reported, and he was sentenced the next month. He had denied the allegations.

Von Einem received a life sentence. The sentencing judge said public outrage created by the crime "must be assuaged and the minds of parents and adolescents must be set at rest", and that its "horrendous nature" of the crime had "added a new dimension to murder committed in this state", the ABC reported. The non-parole period was set at 24 years. In March 1985, on appeal, the then chief justice, Len King, raised it to 36 years, citing the "enormity and depravity of the crime".
The Albany Advertiser likewise describes a non-parole period of 24 years, later increased to 36 following an appeal.

Kelvin was the fifth victim in a series that, in the ABC's account, began in 1979. Before him, the ABC said, came Barnes, aged 17, Muir, 25, Stogneff, 14, and Langley, 18, each killed between 1979 and 1982. Police suspected that more than one person was involved. The group got its nickname after a detective spoke in a 1988 television interview about breaking up the "happy family" thought to be responsible. It has been speculated, the ABC wrote, that the group included members of the state's elite. That is a theory, not a finding.

The killings left a mark on Adelaide. South Australia's chief justice, Chris Kourakis, said that coming after the Beaumont children and the Ratcliffe children, they "unsettled the community" and left a lasting anxiety. The criminologist Xanthé Mallett said it "really rocked the community" and that people still talk about it.

Two other cases touched von Einem or the series directly. A doctor was arrested and charged with Muir's murder but was acquitted after a Supreme Court trial in 1980, according to the ABC. And in 1990, von Einem was himself committed for trial on the murders of Barnes and Langley while serving his sentence. He denied the charges. The charges were dropped after it was ruled that some of the evidence could not be used at trial, the ABC reported. In the Nightly's words, he was charged with two more murders and both were dropped for lack of admissible evidence.
Because of that, he remains the only person convicted of any of the five deaths. For the other four, the ABC said, no one has ever been brought to justice.

In October 2008, South Australia's government doubled the reward in the Family murders to $1 million. Superintendent John Venditto, who was leading a review, said police were looking at four suspects and would consider immunity for one who came forward, since "the one with the least culpability" might find the reward attractive.

A 2020 Crime Stoppers report, quoted by the ABC, said investigators "are convinced that more than one person was involved in Richard's murder". The million-dollar reward for others involved in Kelvin's death was still on offer in 2026.
content.h2: Behind bars, and the law written for him
content.p: The ABC dated his first contact with police to May 1972, when he drove an injured man, Roger James, to the Royal Adelaide Hospital after James had been thrown into the River Torrens. That is the only detail the ABC gave of his life before 1983.

Inside, he was moved from Yatala to Port Augusta Prison in 2007. That year, on 1 November, he became eligible to apply for parole after 24 years. The Correctional Services Department said it had received no application from him, and he never made one. Premier Mike Rann repeated a vow that he would never leave prison alive. New laws that took effect the same day allowed the government to ask the Supreme Court to remove a non-parole period for any prisoner classed as a "dangerous offender". Attorney-General Michael Atkinson said von Einem did not appear to be contrite, was not co-operating with inquiries into related murders and had not used the sex-offender rehabilitation programs on offer. Rann later said von Einem would be the first test case for the law.

In June 2009 a magistrate sentenced him to three months' jail for possessing child pornography in his cell, the ABC reported. Police had found three handwritten stories about sex between boys and men in his cell in 2005. The magistrate accepted that he had kept them under his bed as insurance against the prisoner who wrote them, after threats were made. The court was told his fingerprints were not on the pages and that the stories were in a sealed envelope. The ABC said he was declared a dangerous offender in 2009.

On 24 November 2025 the ABC reported that von Einem had been moved from Port Augusta to the infirmary at Yatala because he had little time left. Court documents later showed he was diagnosed with lung cancer in September 2025. Nine News reported that two major crime detectives visited him on 28 November; police would not confirm that an interview took place, and 9News said it was unclear what, if anything, he told them. In the Premier's words, SA Police had been "working exceptionally hard to get information out of von Einem right up until his death".

Premier Peter Malinauskas said von Einem was found dead in the early hours of Saturday 6 December during a routine round of checks. In a statement he called his life "defined by calculated brutality" and said he "chose silence, callous, deliberate silence, denying victims' families even the faintest chance of closure". The Albany Advertiser said he was believed to have died on the Friday; the ABC and the Premier's account place the finding on the Saturday.

Others reacted bluntly. The state's deputy premier said every day that person was not on the planet was a good day. The Commissioner for Victims' Rights, Sarah Quick, said some families might feel a small sense of relief, but that his refusal to provide any information had denied them closure and complicated their grief.

The State Coroner, David Whittle, delivered findings on 28 August 2026. He found that von Einem died of "metastatic malignancy on a background of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, atherosclerotic vascular disease and Type 2 diabetes", and that he had been given medical care of a high standard. Departing from custom, he made no remarks about von Einem's life, saying that to look for positive aspects would be "neither appropriate nor productive".
The ABC reported that medical notes recorded von Einem as "falling asleep mid-sentence" the day before he was found dead. He had told a doctor he was willing to look at treatment options.
